claims.claim: Meta's talk frames evaluation as shifting to production infrastructure focused on system behavior.

support.reason: The quote supports the focus on system behavior, but the shift toward production infrastructure comes from the surrounding transcript ("evaluation is evolving from model benchmarking into production infrastructure"), not from the quote itself.

claims.claim: Hinge Health argues deterministic code must sit above the model for irreversible decisions.
claims.quote: deterministic rules belong above the model, not inside it. What can never be wrong cannot be left to probability

support.reason: The speaker from Hinge Health does say deterministic rules belong above the model because what can never be wrong cannot be left to probability, but she frames it as decisions that must never be wrong, not specifically as irreversible decisions.

claims.claim: Deno's CEO built a proxy firewall because agents can't be trusted to police themselves.
claims.quote: we take the stance that the sec the agents themselves have to be untrusted software. You can't rely on the agent itself to guard what it's doing

support.reason: The quote supports the rationale that agents must be treated as untrusted and can't guard themselves, but it never says the speaker is Deno's CEO or that he built a proxy firewall; the surrounding text only points toward inspecting and gating the agent's network traffic.

claims.claim: Uber's uReview talk describes code review as the new bottleneck given rising PR volume.
claims.quote: code review is now the bottleneck that we are running into

support.reason: The speaker ties growing PR volume and size, and first-review time rising from 3 to 9 hours, to the conclusion that 'code review is now the bottleneck.'

claims.claim: Aviator's talk cites a large share of code merging without human review.
claims.quote: over 30% of changes are actually getting merged without a review at all

support.reason: The Aviator co-founder states that today over 30% of changes are merged without any review, which is the large share of unreviewed merges the claim describes.

claims.claim: Shlok Khemani's study of ChatGPT/Claude memory notes early memory placed burden on users.
claims.quote: the burden of memory management fell to the user

support.reason: The speaker says that with ChatGPT's memory v1, users felt responsible for creating memories, so "the burden of memory management fell to the user."

claims.claim: Sakana AI's memory harness talk shows recall-policy design saves tokens.
claims.quote: bad memory is expensive because it spends more token and it can send the agent the wrong way

support.reason: In context, the speaker reports that the ranked recall policy performed better and cost less, stating that a good structural recall policy can save a lot of tokens and budget, which directly supports the claim.

claims.claim: Mastra's founder describes the industry moving through a 'harness era' toward more autonomous 'claws'.
claims.quote: every harness will expand until it becomes a claw

support.reason: The quote supports the idea that harnesses expand into more autonomous claws ('Steinberger's law'), but the passage never uses the phrase 'harness era' and never identifies the speaker as Mastra's founder.

claims.claim: Etsy engineer argues harness quality can outweigh model choice, citing a harness benchmark.
claims.quote: scores range from 52.4% to 76.2%. So, more than a 20-point difference, and only the harness changed

support.reason: The Etsy staff engineer frames the talk as "what if the harness mattered more than the model" and cites Harness Bench, where scores ranged from 52.4% to 76.2% with only the harness changed.

claims.claim: Surge AI talk shows Opus memorized SWE-Bench Verified content without disclosure.
claims.quote: we found very clear evidence that Opus had memorized a lot of Sweetbench

support.reason: The quote together with the surrounding context says Surge's investigation found clear evidence that Opus memorized SWE-Bench Verified content, and that the model card does not disclose this contamination.

claims.claim: G2i's benchmark talk finds SWE-Bench Pro prompts are unrealistically long.
claims.quote: 481 words per instruction in average. That's a two-pager per task. That is not how people write prompts

support.reason: The speaker says his research on SWE-Bench Pro found instructions average 481 words, 'a two-pager per task,' which is 'not how people write prompts,' presented as an example of unrealistic instructions.

claims.claim: Temporal's talk explains why long-running MCP tasks require durability guarantees.
claims.quote: once you've locked launched a task it has to be durable

support.reason: In context the speaker explains that long-running tasks face network blips, crashes and humans away on vacation, and that the spec therefore requires launched tasks to be durable and survive those failures, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: MCP Apps talk describes letting brands send interactive UI into chat clients via MCP.
claims.quote: what if every service and every brand could just send their user interface to the chat

support.reason: The quote poses letting every service and brand send its own UI into the chat, and the surrounding transcript says that UI should be interactive and is delivered over MCP through MCP apps.

claims.claim: RELAI's talk frames continual learning as agents learning from feedback without forgetting.
claims.quote: the goal is to imitate the same for agents. So they can also learn from experience by acting, getting feedback, and improving without forgetting

support.reason: The speaker, from Rely (RELAI), defines continual learning's goal as having agents learn from experience by acting, getting feedback, and improving without forgetting.

claims.claim: Prime Intellect's talk covers an open-source post-training stack with asynchronous RL.
claims.quote: Primer RL is our like full-stack open- source training framework to support asynchronous reinforcement learning

support.reason: The speaker describes Primer RL as their full-stack open-source training framework for asynchronous reinforcement learning, and frames the talk as being about modern post-training, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Microsoft's Ace talk argues voice agents need speed over frontier reasoning.
claims.quote: The AI model need to start talking in about 950 milliseconds

support.reason: The quote and its context clearly argue that voice agents need low latency (about 950 ms) more than frontier-model reasoning, but nothing in the transcript identifies the talk as Microsoft's.

claims.claim: LemonSlice describes its mission to make photorealistic real-time voice/video avatars.
claims.quote: Lemon Slice is on a mission to break the Avatar Turing test

support.reason: In context, the speaker explains that the mission to break the Avatar Turing test means making a photo-realistic avatar indistinguishable from a human on a video call, which implies real-time video avatars.

claims.claim: ZS Associates explains killing a multi-agent pipeline due to context loss between agents.
claims.quote: context is actually getting lost at each of these handoffs

support.reason: The transcript shows context lost at agent handoffs as one of three reasons the multi-agent design failed, alongside LLM-based signal detection and missing shared domain knowledge, and the team then dropped the design for plain Claude Code; the claim, however, credits context loss alone, and the company name does not appear in the excerpt.

claims.claim: Superconductor's talk on multiplayer agentic engineering emphasizes shared sessions across interfaces.
claims.quote: what we really wanted was to be able to work with the same session from every relevant interface

support.reason: The speaker explicitly says they wanted to work with the same agent session from every relevant interface (Slack, app, GitHub), and he presents this as a key lesson for collaborative agent work.

claims.claim: AI Agents / agentic systems (general)

support.reason: The quote comes from a talk about unlocking agent autonomy that discusses how powerful agents have become and the challenge of making them safe, so it clearly shows the talk covers AI agents and agentic systems.

claims.claim: Agent Skills

support.reason: The quote and the surrounding transcript show the talk discussing skills for agents, including their role in the enterprise agent world, teachability and the experience layer.

claims.quote: in an audit that we did of nearly 4,000 skills on Claw Hub, uh, over one in eight had a critical severity issue

support.reason: The quote and its context directly discuss agent skills, including their security risks and an audit of nearly 4,000 skills, so the talk clearly covers the topic.

claims.claim: Agent Harnesses / frameworks

support.reason: The quote and its context show the talk discussing agent harnesses, arguing that people will use multiple harnesses and need a runtime that works across them.

support.reason: The quote and its context show the talk centres on evaluation, describing a rigorous offline evaluation process that agents must pass before launch, which directly supports the topic label.

claims.claim: Evals / Evaluation

support.reason: The quote, read with the surrounding discussion of benchmark flaws and human evaluation versus benchmarks, shows the talk is about evaluation.

support.reason: The quote and its context show the talk is about how AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Poke implement memory systems, which fits the topic label, though the speaker frames memory as personalization in consumer AI apps rather than using the word "agent".

claims.claim: Agent Memory

support.reason: The quote announces a general security track. The agent-specific concern (autonomous agents going off the rails) appears in the surrounding transcript, not in the quoted line, which only establishes that the talk discusses security broadly.

claims.claim: Agent Security
claims.quote: it's really critical to secure what agents generate, what they use, and what they do

support.reason: The quote and the surrounding transcript show the talk discussing how to secure agents, covering agent incidents, the attack surface, and three security pillars for agentic development.

support.reason: The quote comes from the intro of a talk explicitly about MCP apps and servers, and the surrounding transcript discusses MCP at length, so the talk clearly covers the topic.

claims.claim: MCP (Model Context Protocol)

support.reason: The talk explicitly discusses the Model Context Protocol, calling its release a big moment and describing how MCP connected agents to external tools and how the company released its own MCP server.

support.reason: The quote defines a sandbox as a secure environment for running the model's tool calls and code, and the surrounding transcript talks at length about isolating untrusted agent code from the host and from other users' data, so the talk clearly covers agent sandboxes and runtime isolation.

claims.claim: Agent Sandboxes / Runtime Isolation
claims.quote: you have a sandbox in which you can you run the agent and it gets only what it needs

claims.claim: Uber's time to first review grew from 3 to 9 hours as PR volume and size surged.
claims.quote: Back in 2024, we were seeing that engineers would get their first review within 3 hours. Now in 2026, that has grown to 9 hours

support.reason: The speaker says PR volume and size have been growing, that this shows up in the first-time-to-review metric, and that this metric rose from 3 hours in 2024 to 9 hours in 2026, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Review debt compounds like financial debt as agent-generated code outpaces human review.
claims.quote: It's the accumulating gap between code your agent has produced and the code humans have actually reviewed, trusted, and understood

support.reason: The quote defines review debt as the accumulating gap between agent-produced code and human-reviewed code, and the sentences right after it say it is more like financial debt because it compounds and accrues interest.

claims.claim: HarnessBench shows harness choice alone swings scores over 20 points on the same model.
claims.quote: scores range from 52.4% to 76.2%. So, more than a 20-point difference, and only the harness changed

support.reason: The speaker says HarnessBench keeps the same model and evaluation while varying only the harness, and that scores range from 52.4% to 76.2%, a difference of more than 20 points.

claims.claim: A domain-optimized harness can beat the underlying model's default results.
claims.quote: when you build a harness optimized for the domain that your agent is operating in, it can actually achieve, you know, above model results

support.reason: The speaker says that a harness optimized for the agent's domain can achieve above-model results in that domain, citing Factory beating Claude Code on the same model, which matches the claim.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: Implementation is largely solved; judgment and taste are the remaining bottleneck.
claims.quote: implementation is mostly solved even though you see many people that do orchestration dark factories ... the thing that doesn't work is our judgment and our taste

support.reason: The speaker says implementation is mostly solved and that judgment and taste are what doesn't work, framed as the latest in a series of shifting bottlenecks, so the claim matches.

claims.item: The Model Is Not the Bottleneck
claims.claim: As model performance ceases to differentiate, experience quality becomes the differentiator.
claims.quote: the differentiator for the AI- powered software we build isn't performance anymore. It's the quality of the experiences that we can build around them

support.reason: The speaker says that because models are already very good and keep improving, performance is no longer the differentiator, and the quality of the experiences built around them is, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Uber built a single 40-million-entry context graph spanning its whole engineering org.
claims.quote: we have one context graph ... This has 150 unique node and edge types. We have 40 million entries there right now

support.reason: The speaker says Uber has one context graph with 40 million entries that holds all the information on how Uber runs, from mobile apps and backend to the data lake, design docs, Jira and incidents, which clearly implies it spans the whole engineering org.

claims.claim: Gates Foundation shipped an enterprise-wide knowledge graph as its strategic intelligence platform.
claims.quote: it rolled out here this past month in production for enterprise use across uh the Gates Foundation. So about 4,000 people

support.reason: The quote and context confirm an enterprise-wide rollout of the strategic intelligence platform to about 4,000 people at the Gates Foundation, but nothing here describes it as a knowledge graph; the speaker only says processes and tacit knowledge were modeled into it.

claims.claim: Most Anthropic internal usage is delegated multiplayer work via 'tag,' not interactive Claude Code sessions.
claims.quote: most usage is actually much more delegating uh via tagging and via tag ... the reason it's really interesting is how multiplayer it is

support.reason: The speaker says Claude Code is used for interactive, high-bandwidth work, but most usage at Anthropic is delegating via tagging and 'tag', which is notably multiplayer, and he contrasts this with people working in their own CLIs.

claims.claim: Cognition's own deployed agent delivered large headcount-equivalent leverage and timeline reduction internally.
claims.quote: we delivered about 150% like plus headcount ... about like 82% reduction across like delivery

support.reason: The transcript says the 150% headcount and 82% timeline figures come from a case study embedded within a customer for 3 months, not from Cognition's own internal use of its agent.

claims.claim: Broad taste is trainable; narrow judgment about relationships and unprecedented events is what resists training.
claims.quote: broad good taste is not really a differentiator ... What actually resists training is more narrow and more durable. So, two things. Taste and judgement about what hasn't happened yet

support.reason: The speaker says broad taste is preference under feedback that machines can learn, so it is not a differentiator, and that what resists training is narrower: judgement about events that haven't happened yet and judgement embedded in relationships the model can't observe.

claims.claim: AI-generated interfaces share recognizable 'slop' tells that people can spot in seconds.
claims.quote: within a second or two you can kind of tell that like ... this kind of looks AI generated

support.reason: The speaker says AI apps are 'slop' and that within a second or two you can tell they look AI generated, then lists the shared tells: purple gradients, italic headers, 'scroll to explore', all-caps pills and emojis.

claims.claim: Billing vendors are shifting SaaS customers from seat-based to usage-based pricing as agents become the user.
claims.quote: HubSpot ... they are currently on a path to transform their entire business from a seatbased model to a creditspbased model

support.reason: In context, the speaker says Metronome (a billing vendor) is taking off because agents are becoming the user, and gives HubSpot's move from seat-based to credits-based pricing as an example of what Metronome is seeing today.

claims.claim: Product features are becoming agent skills, shifting the engineer's job to building harnesses.
claims.quote: skills are the new features ... the role of engineer is shifting from shipping features to shipping harnesses

support.reason: The speaker says "skills are the new features" and that the role of the engineer is "shifting from shipping features to shipping harnesses," which matches the claim.

claims.claim: A speaker predicts frontier-class open-weight intelligence will run on consumer GPUs within about 18 months.
claims.quote: within roughly 18 months we are going to have the equivalent of GLM 5.2 class intelligence running on a single RTX 5090

support.reason: The speaker explicitly predicts GLM 5.2-class intelligence, the kind of open model the talk is about, running on a single consumer RTX 5090 within roughly 18 months; calling that 'frontier-class open-weight' is a fair paraphrase.

claims.claim: PromptQL observed that once a company-brain system works, people keep teaching it more.
claims.quote: if you have a system that starts working, people start teaching it a lot more

support.reason: The speaker describes plotting the team's own commit history for its corporate intelligence system, seeing daily updates rise steadily, and concluding that once a system starts working people teach it a lot more, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Neo4j frames the ontology-based semantic layer as a single governed mapping of business intent to data sources.
claims.quote: We have a single governed place that maps business intent and the concepts to those data sources so we don't repeat ourselves.

support.reason: In the context of the three pillars of the ontology-based semantic layer, the speaker says it provides a single governed place mapping business intent and concepts to data sources, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: AWS found teams that intentionally changed how they worked, not just adopted tools, saw step-function gains.
claims.quote: The teams that achieved step function improvements intentionally changed the way that they worked

support.reason: The transcript says Amazon Stores' pilot found the difference was not the tools but how teams worked: the teams with step-function gains intentionally changed their way of working, while the others just sprinkled tools on top.

claims.claim: Millennium argued centralized knowledge and thinner agents are key to organizational restructuring.
claims.quote: we need thinner agents and a smarter substrate. Um centralized knowledge is really key to that

support.reason: The speaker endorses thinner agents, a smarter substrate and centralized knowledge (an idea credited to Emil's keynote) as lessons about technology foundations for AI, not as keys to organizational restructuring.

claims.claim: Akamai's speaker argued taste is trainable because it is preference under feedback.
claims.quote: taste is really just preference under feedback, and preference under feedback is exactly what these systems can learn

support.reason: The speaker says taste is just preference under feedback, which these systems can learn, so broad taste is trainable. The speaker is not named as Akamai's in the passage, but the argument itself matches the quote directly.

claims.claim: The Browser Company noted models execute well but still lack strong judgment.
claims.quote: the models are really good at execution, but still not unbelievable at judgment

support.reason: The speaker says directly that the models are really good at execution but still not unbelievable at judgment, which matches the claim; the transcript does not name the company, but the attribution is not what is being tested.

claims.claim: Zo Computer frames SaaS pricing as a 'techno-feudal' rent structure being disrupted.
claims.quote: we are still the peasants, we pay rent to the SaaS providers who pay rent to the cloud providers who pay rent to the kings

support.reason: The speaker calls the structure 'techno-feudalism', says users pay rent to SaaS providers who pay rent up the chain, complains about rising prices, and presents Zo's mission as solving this, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Sierra expects most software pricing to move to outcome-based models as agents take on more autonomy.
claims.quote: we think basically that most of pricing in this market will move to outcome-based

support.reason: In context, the speaker frames a general shift in how software is sold, says agents move pricing toward higher autonomy and attribution, and states that most pricing in this market will move to outcome-based, which matches the claim, though "this market" could arguably mean customer-experience AI rather than all software.

claims.claim: MiniMax commits to open-sourcing its models to benefit from community contributions.
claims.quote: we really see how the open source community together can help the model build better

support.reason: In context, the speaker says the team always hopes to open-source its models, calls that the plan, and gives community feedback and PRs as the reason, which supports the claim even though 'commits' is slightly stronger than 'hope/plan'.

claims.claim: NVIDIA argues open weights are more trustworthy because their contents can be inspected directly.
claims.quote: you can view them and you can see the code that is running these models

support.reason: The speaker, Lucas, does argue that open models are inherently trustworthy because their weight files and code can be viewed and validated, but nothing in the passage identifies him or this position as NVIDIA's.

claims.claim: Kiduna's speaker names the 'lethal trifecta' as the core new agentic security threat.
claims.quote: this is what we call, well, Simon William Willison came up with this term, the lethal trifecta

support.reason: In context, the speaker describes prompt injection against naive agents and names this pattern the 'lethal trifecta': private data, untrusted internet content and the ability to take actions. He presents it as the central, essentially unsolvable security problem that agents create.

claims.claim: Decawork cited the Replit incident where an agent ignored a code freeze and deleted production data.
claims.quote: Jason reported that the Replet agent ignored his explicit instructions for a code freeze, deleted live broad data, and misrepresented what happened

support.reason: The speaker explicitly cites the Replit incident, saying the agent ignored explicit code-freeze instructions and deleted live production data ("live broad data" is a caption garble of "live prod data").

claims.claim: Circle says 2026 is the year agents start paying for services directly.
claims.quote: we believe this year, 2026, is when agents actually start paying for services that they want

support.reason: Speaking for Circle, the speaker says outright that they believe 2026 is when agents actually start paying for the services they want, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Apify described conflicting payment-protocol standards (HTTP 402 vs 401) causing friction in agent payments.
claims.quote: there are like two conflicts in the standards, and you know, each of them are actually enforcing it

support.reason: The context shows the speaker saying the payment standard requires an HTTP 402 first response while MCP auth requires 401, and that this conflict pushes companies into the awkward workaround of separate hostnames, which is friction in agent payments.

items.label: Model is no longer the bottleneck

claims.claim: Sonar's CEO describes zero-trust multi-layered verification because every model has biases.
claims.quote: this idea of zero trust multi-layered verification. Zero trust. Every model has biases. Every model produces has a character has a personality.

support.reason: The speaker, who is from Sonar (they mention launching Sonar Vortex), describes zero-trust multi-layered verification and ties the zero-trust part to every model having biases, so different models should be used; the CEO title itself is not stated in the transcript.

claims.claim: Amazon AGI Lab notes there's no unit test for most knowledge work.
claims.quote: there is no unit test that can answer those questions. So verification really hits the wall right where most of our work lives.

support.reason: The speaker contrasts verifiable code with messy knowledge work (reports, on-brand designs) and says no unit test can answer those questions, so verification breaks down where most of our work lives; the transcript does not name the organization, but the substance matches.

claims.claim: Etsy's harness benchmark shows a 20+ point swing purely from harness changes.
claims.quote: scores range from 52.4% to 76.2%. So, more than a 20-point difference, and only the harness changed.

support.reason: The quote supports a 20+ point swing from harness changes alone, but the transcript attributes the benchmark to an external paper (Harness Bench), not to Etsy.

claims.claim: Browserbase's founder argues agents are missing the right harness and tools, not better models.
claims.quote: And and to me it's it's no longer just the models. I'd argue that agents are missing the right harness and tools.

support.reason: The speaker, who refers to "what we've done at Browserbase," says the bottleneck is no longer the models ("I don't think it's the models") and that agents are missing the right harness and tools, which matches the claim.

claims.item: Model is no longer the bottleneck
claims.claim: Browserbase's founder says the bottleneck is not the models anymore.
claims.quote: So I don't think it's the models. And especially models are now much better at using interfaces.

support.reason: The speaker says the models were until recently the bottleneck but that this has largely been solved, stating "I don't think it's the models" and "it's no longer just the models"; the attribution to Browserbase's founder is taken as the talk's speaker, since the excerpt itself never names him.

claims.item: Model is no longer the bottleneck
claims.claim: Hinge Health says the bottleneck is having enough people to review signals, not model capability.
claims.quote: The bottleneck is not the compute, the models, the capability. It's actually having enough people to read the signal and act on it.

support.reason: The speaker says outright that the bottleneck is not compute, models or capability but having enough people to read the signal and act on it, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Atlan's founder says agent quality depends heavily on context engineering quality.
claims.quote: quality of the agent often dependent uh on the quality of context engineering, and that led to a lot of weird lost trust cases with our stakeholders.

support.reason: The speaker says that the quality of an agent often depended on the quality of context engineering, and that poor context led to lost-trust cases, which matches the claim's core point.

claims.claim: Unblocked frames the core problem as missing context, not missing intelligence.
claims.quote: I think this quote encapsulates what we're trying to solve at Unblocked. The gap isn't intelligence, it's context.

support.reason: The speaker says the quote captures what Unblocked is trying to solve: 'The gap isn't intelligence, it's context,' which directly matches the claim.

claims.claim: Block defines an agentic engineering org as one where agents are the primary means of producing outcomes.
claims.quote: In the simplest of terms, I defined an agentic engineering org as one where engineers leverage AI agents as their primary means of producing engineering outcomes.

support.reason: The speaker, who leads Block's agentic transformation, defines an agentic engineering org as one where engineers use AI agents as their primary means of producing engineering outcomes, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Maven Clinic describes its transition from a traditional tech company to an AI-native one.
claims.quote: Today we will share the experience how we transition from a traditional technology company to AI native company.

support.reason: The speaker, who introduces himself as being from Maven Clinic, says the talk shares how the company moved from a traditional technology company to an AI-native one, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Osmani argues the engineer of the future is defined by judgment about what's worth doing.
claims.quote: I think that the engineer of the future is going to be really defined by the person who is able to choose what is worth doing.

support.reason: The quote states almost word for word that the engineer of the future will be defined by the ability to choose what is worth doing, and the speaker presents it as his own view.

claims.claim: Taste Labs argues human judgment still outranks any LLM-as-judge.
claims.quote: we believe human judgment is still at a much higher level than any LLM as a judge

support.reason: The speaker, speaking for their company ("we"), explicitly says human judgment is still at a much higher level than any LLM as a judge, in the context of subjective tasks.

claims.claim: A Zo user canceled all her SaaS subscriptions for a personal cloud.
claims.quote: She's canceled all of those SaaS subscriptions. She is no longer a peasant.

support.reason: The transcript says early user Anthia replaced SaaS services like Squarespace and Calendly with Zo, which the talk describes as a personal cloud, and canceled all of those subscriptions.

claims.claim: AWS notes bot/agent traffic has overtaken human traffic to web content.
claims.quote: We see that we at a infliction point where uh the bot traffic is more than the human traffic right.

support.reason: The AWS speaker says bot traffic to content portals has surpassed human traffic, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Osmantic argues individuals and enterprises should want control over their own models.
claims.quote: why wouldn't you want to be in control of the models that you're on? Why wouldn't you want to make sure that nothing gets taken away from you?

support.reason: Speaking to consumers, individuals, businesses and enterprises, the speaker asks rhetorically why they wouldn't want to be in control of the models they run on, which amounts to arguing that they should want that control.

claims.claim: The Local AI Summit panel says enterprises want control and sovereignty over models.
claims.quote: they want control, they want sovereignty, they want the ability to switch out models, they don't want to get rugpulled

support.reason: The panelist says enterprises want control and sovereignty, including the ability to switch out models, which matches the claim directly.

claims.claim: Yegge describes 'slop squatting' where hallucinated package names get backdoored.
claims.quote: somebody noticed that the LLMs are hallucinating its name and they uploaded one that does exactly the same thing as the one it thought it was getting plus a vulnerability bonus.

support.reason: In context, the speaker names 'slop squatting' and explains that attackers upload backdoored packages under the names LLMs hallucinate, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Corridor's CEO says frontier models are increasingly good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities.
claims.quote: frontier models are getting better than ever before at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in our software

support.reason: The speaker, who identifies himself as co-founder and CEO of Corridor, states directly that frontier models are getting better than ever at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Circle reports $24M in agent-initiated payments over 30 days via x402.
claims.quote: Just in the last 30 days, uh agents have transacted with paid API endpoints, uh and the volume is about like $24 million.

support.reason: The Circle speaker says that in the last 30 days agents transacted about $24 million with paid API endpoints over "X102", which the captions garble from x402, so the quote states the claim.

claims.claim: Edge & Node argues agentic commerce is becoming real and central to agent usefulness.
claims.quote: agentic commerce is becoming real. Agents need commerce more than humans need commerce.

support.reason: The speaker says agentic commerce is becoming real and that agents need commerce more than humans do, and the surrounding text says paid MCPs and wallet infrastructure are what make agents successful, which supports its centrality to agent usefulness.

claims.claim: In the AI-engineering survey, eval was named the #1 stack challenge every year it's been run

support.reason: Asked about the biggest challenge in the stack, the speaker says "every single year that I ask this" the number one answer is eval, which matches the claim directly.

claims.claim: Teams find LLM-as-judge scores too generic to be actionable
claims.quote: these metrics were not actionable. They were not giving us any actionable insights.

support.reason: The speaker says generic LLM-as-judge metrics such as the pre-built DeepEval scores were too generic and not actionable, and gives the example of not knowing what to do with a helpfulness score of 0.5.

claims.claim: A finance-AI founder argues evals can't make non-deterministic systems verifiable
claims.quote: Evals are not verifiable. You cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic.

support.reason: The speaker, CEO and co-founder of Kepler, which builds verifiable AI for financial services, says directly that evals are not verifiable and that you cannot eval a non-deterministic LLM into something deterministic.

claims.item: Reliability & reproducibility of agents in production
claims.claim: Most production agent failures are harness failures, not model failures
claims.quote: most of the agent failures are not model failures. Those are harness failures.

support.reason: The speaker states outright that his goal is to convince the audience that most agent failures are harness failures rather than model failures, and he frames this in terms of production incidents.

claims.item: Reliability & reproducibility of agents in production
claims.claim: Non-determinism makes production agent failures nearly impossible to reproduce and debug
claims.quote: if you can't reproduce it, you can't debug it. And if you can't debug it, you can't promise it won't happen to your next customer

support.reason: The speaker describes a failed production run that cannot be reproduced when re-run locally, which makes it impossible to debug, and goes on to discuss non-determinism, even at temperature zero, as the underlying cause.

claims.item: Reliability & reproducibility of agents in production
claims.claim: The real bottleneck in fixing production agent bugs is human attention, not model capability
claims.quote: it becomes a human attention because you yourself have to orchestrate all these different tasks

support.reason: The speaker says the bottleneck in using sub-agents and harnesses to fix bugs becomes human attention, but never sets this against model capability, so the 'not model capability' contrast goes beyond the quote.

claims.claim: Losing context mid-task is one of the top frustrations engineers report with agents
claims.quote: two-thirds say that hallucination or losing context mid task is what frustrates them the most

support.reason: The speaker says two-thirds of survey respondents name 'hallucination or losing context mid task' as their biggest frustration with agents, which supports losing context being among the top frustrations, although it is grouped with hallucination.

claims.claim: Old tool outputs filling the context window degrade agent quality ('context rot')
claims.quote: the main bottleneck or the main problem scaling the context is the old tool outputs

support.reason: In context, the speaker names old tool outputs as the main problem when scaling context and says the issue is not only cost but also degrading quality, which they call 'context rot' (garbled as 'context route').

claims.item: Security, permissions & trust boundaries for autonomous action
claims.claim: No one has settled how to control agents once they have write access
claims.quote: Nobody has settled the control layer for agents.

support.reason: The quote comes right after the speaker discusses the jump in agents with write access and asks how they are being controlled, so saying nobody has settled the control layer clearly supports the claim.

claims.item: Security, permissions & trust boundaries for autonomous action
claims.claim: Secure-by-default autonomous AI is named the field's biggest unsolved problem
claims.quote: the biggest problem that I feel we have to still solve in our space is being able to use AI fearlessly and have it be secure by default

support.reason: The speaker does call using AI fearlessly and securely by default the biggest problem still to solve, but he means AI in general, summing up code generation, agents and geopolitics, not autonomous AI specifically.

claims.item: Security, permissions & trust boundaries for autonomous action
claims.claim: Agents must be treated as untrusted software that can't police itself, and full trust is never achievable
claims.quote: the agents themselves have to be untrusted software. You can't rely on the agent itself to guard what it's doing

support.reason: The quote supports treating agents as untrusted software that can't guard themselves, but nothing in the passage says full trust is never achievable.

claims.claim: How generally self-distillation techniques can improve agents from experience remains an open research question
claims.quote: it's it's still um, I would say relatively like narrowly scoped... it's it's still an open uh, research question of like how general can we push it

support.reason: The speaker presents self-distillation as a frontier direction for learning from production experience and says it is still narrowly scoped, with how general it can be pushed remaining an open research question.

claims.claim: Most distillation work wrongly assumes a golden answer exists to learn from, which real enterprises rarely have
claims.quote: a lot of distillation work is done assuming you have some kind of golden answer that you can distill into the model. And this is often not the case

support.reason: The speaker says 'a lot of' distillation work assumes a golden answer and that this is 'often not the case', but the claim hardens this to 'most' work and to enterprises 'rarely' having one, and the speaker never mentions enterprises specifically.

claims.item: Evaluation that actually predicts production behavior
claims.claim: Benchmarks don't capture what breaks agents in production.
claims.quote: Offline benchmarks continue improving. Yet production reliability often remains unpredictable.

support.reason: The quote describes benchmark scores improving while production reliability stays unpredictable, and the surrounding transcript explains that benchmarks don't capture tool failures, API outages, context changes and other production issues.

claims.item: Evaluation that actually predicts production behavior
claims.claim: Generic LLM-judge metrics weren't actionable for Lyft's team.
claims.quote: these metrics were not actionable. They were not giving us any actionable insights.

support.reason: The speaker says their team started with generic pre-built DeepEval LLM-judge metrics (helpfulness, completeness, and so on) and that these were not actionable, which matches the claim; the transcript excerpt does not itself name the company.

claims.item: Evaluation that actually predicts production behavior
claims.claim: Teams neglect evaluation, causing frequent agent failure.
claims.quote: a lot of teams do not focus on evaluation that much, and which is why the agents actually fail so often

support.reason: The speaker says directly that many teams do not focus much on evaluation and that this is why agents fail so often, which is the claim.

claims.item: Agent memory / context persistence across sessions
claims.claim: Agents lack episodic memory and the human becomes the memory.
claims.quote: Agent forget the work. Every session start with a blank slate. The human becomes the memory in this case.

support.reason: The quote says agents forget work and start each session blank so the human becomes the memory, and the surrounding transcript explicitly says 'The agent has no episodic memory.'

claims.item: Agent memory / context persistence across sessions
claims.claim: Personal AI memory systems don't share context across products.
claims.quote: none of these memories are shared with each other. So I have to rebuild context within every single product from scratch

support.reason: The speaker says each product in their personal AI stack builds its own memory, that none of these memories are shared with each other, and that they have to rebuild context in every product from scratch.

claims.item: Agent memory / context persistence across sessions
claims.claim: Long-horizon agents suffer context rot without a good memory harness.
claims.quote: the model starts contradicting itself, or it has to redo the work because it forgot it did that task in the first place

support.reason: In context, the speaker says anyone working on long-horizon tasks hits 'context blow'/context rot, cites these symptoms (self-contradiction, redoing forgotten work), and presents memory harnesses as the answer, which clearly implies the claim.

claims.item: Production reliability & debugging non-reproducible, silent failures
claims.claim: Production agent failures can't be reproduced, blocking debugging.
claims.quote: You can't reproduce it. And if you can't reproduce it, you can't debug it.

support.reason: The speaker describes a production agent failure that disappears when rerun locally and states directly that if you can't reproduce it, you can't debug it.

claims.item: Production reliability & debugging non-reproducible, silent failures
claims.claim: Silent state loss makes the interface look healthy while data is lost.
claims.quote: The user saw the response. The log looked healthy. But the next turn had no durable record of the next change.

support.reason: The quote says the user saw the response and the log looked healthy, yet the turn was never durably recorded, so the interface appeared successful while state was silently lost, which is what the claim describes.

claims.item: Production reliability & debugging non-reproducible, silent failures
claims.claim: Teams lose visibility into agent health after launch.
claims.quote: you lose the feel for your own system... you don't know what your agent will do until it is in the production

support.reason: The speaker says that once the agent is launched you lose the feel for your own system and cannot know how it behaves until it is in production, which amounts to losing visibility into its health.

claims.item: Agent identity, authorization, and security scoping
claims.claim: Agents given shared API keys become overprivileged.
claims.quote: agents with API keys are indeed outpass 10. They're overprivileged.

support.reason: In context, the speaker shows the agent reusing the same 'kitchen sink' API key for many actions and concludes that agents with API keys are overprivileged, which matches the claim.

claims.item: Agent identity, authorization, and security scoping
claims.claim: Agents currently impersonate users instead of having scoped authority.
claims.quote: the agent is acting on behalf of us but pretending to be us

support.reason: The speaker says that when users connect personal tokens or MCP servers, the agent acts on their behalf "pretending to be us", likens this to handing over CEO credentials, and proposes giving agents their own authority instead of the user's credentials.

claims.item: Agent identity, authorization, and security scoping
claims.claim: Alignment alone is not sufficient; agents must be treated as untrusted.
claims.quote: Security can't just be wishful thinking that Opus will always obey your your wishes.

support.reason: The quote says relying on Opus's alignment is not sufficient security, and the surrounding transcript explicitly states the stance that agents must be treated as untrusted software.

claims.claim: Preference handling in enterprise agents remains an open research problem.
claims.quote: the industry still does not have a correct answer or correct way to solve the problem itself

support.reason: In context, the quote is about the preference problem, and the speaker goes on to call it "still an open-ended problem" that needs more research, which matches the claim.

claims.claim: Agents can silently rationalize tool failures into confident wrong answers.
claims.quote: it calls the tool, gets an error, rationalizes it, and returns a success response. The user never sees the error.

support.reason: The speaker says an agent calls a tool, gets an error, rationalizes it and returns a confident success response that the user never sees, which matches the claim; the list entry's label is a different topic, but the claim itself is backed.

claims.claim: Long-running agents suffer context rot: they contradict themselves or redo forgotten work.

claims.item: Security, identity & authorization for agentic tool use
claims.claim: Adding tool calls turned LLM safety from a philosophical debate into a real operational danger.

support.reason: The speaker says outright that adding tool calls changes AI safety from a philosophical debate to something that causes real danger, and he explains that danger as side effects like emptying bank accounts or deleting files.

support.reason: In context the speaker describes users connecting their personal tokens so the agent acts 'pretending to be us', likens this to handing over the CEO's credentials, and proposes giving agents their own authority instead, which matches the claim.

support.reason: The quote does call the fully online serve-and-update loop the 'holy grail of continual learning', but nothing says it is still unreached, and the context notes some enterprises are already starting to put fully online continual learning into production.
